title: Hands-on: Three Operator Cases
points: Run one notebook to understand three operator studies.
180 minutes / three short exercises / no coding experience required
note: Open Classroom Labs before the workshop. Participants will run fresh numerical calculations and inspect clearly labeled archived model replies. Use the same notebook for all three cases. If devices are limited, work in pairs: one person runs the cells while the other checks the evidence. The deck uses the IEEE ComSoc theme. The classroom cycle is run, change, check and explain. This expanded edition includes a new L10B replay and a proposed control-room advisory pilot. The scheduled teaching time is 180 minutes; allow breaks outside that total. The presenter affiliations are supplied by the presenters. The new Stanford teaching bridge is an adaptation of general reliability ideas, not a claim that the lab implements those Stanford frameworks. Use the six-page Participant Lab Guide for the exact activity steps. The first five slides take five minutes and make the agentic loop explicit before setup. The opening as a whole takes 12 minutes. Case-level replay slides preview saved examples; learners run L10B later in the guided notebook order. Original Stanford lecture figures appear on slides 3, 64, 70 and 71. Adapted grid teaching diagrams cite the relevant lecture page. Full author, title, institution, date, page and reading link appear with the source material.

title: What is agentic AI?
points: An LLM agent works toward a goal by choosing tools, reading their results and choosing what to do next.
note: Use the architectural definition in Anthropic, Building effective agents: an agent lets the LLM direct its process and tool use. Agentic AI is a broad term; here it means a system organized around this bounded loop. An AI agent is the component that chooses and follows steps. A tool is a permitted software function that returns a result. Point to the goal, model choice, executable tool, returned evidence and feedback arrow. The application stores case facts and prior results as the context supplied at the next model request. If a required check is missing, the outcome remains HOLD. Stop or return a proposal only under the fixed workflow rules. Do not imply that feedback alone establishes agency: conventional programs can also branch and loop. Our default notebook calculates engineering results now but replays the actual old Llama choices. No live model service is needed. Stanford source: Monica Lam, CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction, Fall 2026, p.2 describes function calling and agentic workflows. The goal-and-feedback drawing is our grid teaching adaptation, supported by the separate bounded-agent architecture citation. This is not an original Stanford power-system diagram.
caption: Grid teaching adaptation of the Stanford lecture, p.2. Model choices are recorded; calculations can run now.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.2.

title: Stanford: tool calls become a workflow
points: A tool call runs one step. An agentic workflow links steps and uses their results to continue or stop.
note: Show the two original capability panels from Monica Lam’s Stanford CS224V introduction, p.2. The left panel introduces model-selected function calling. The right panel describes multi-step planning, tool use and self-correction. Our plain-language sentence connects the panels to the preceding bounded-loop teaching drawing. The next slide supplies a real recorded grid example. In that example Llama requests a named action and Python validates the JSON choice before calling an existing function; it does not use a native tool_calls protocol. Conventional software can also loop, and a chatbot may itself contain an agent. Here we identify the agentic feature by the model’s permitted next-step choice based on returned evidence. The class replays those old model choices while numerical cells calculate current results. Source lecture figure is shown unchanged within the documented crop.
caption: Original Stanford lecture excerpt, p.2. The next slide connects these ideas to the recorded grid study.

title: A real agent changes its next step
points: The failed tool result leads to a fallback check. Passing the checks still leaves human review.
note: This is an actual saved Llama 3.1:8b voltage episode, not a fabricated interactive exchange. Call 1 selects VERIFY_SAC_FIRST; the numerical check returns 111.966607 percent of allowed current and two current violations. Call 2 selects USE_MPC_PLAN; its numerical check returns 99.604410 percent of allowed current and no recorded violations. The SAC and MPC tools already exist; Llama does not invent or solve the power flow. The arrows show tool-request, result, next-request, result. Call 3 selects REVIEW_EVIDENCE. Human acknowledgment remains PENDING and equipment_dispatch is False. This separate P3 MV/LV OpenDSS archive differs from the fresh L2 exercise and from L3 test_01. Later voltage slides display the exact public returned reasons; learners can replay the source in L10B after completing the three cases. The fixed comparator reaches the same numerical outcome, so the trace illustrates coordination rather than a proven performance improvement.
caption: Recorded P3 example, separate from L2. 111.966607% and 99.604410% are rounded here.

title: Llama chooses; tools calculate; people decide
points: The agent coordinates a study. Numerical tools supply the checks. The operator reviews the proposal.
note: Use the three symbols to assign responsibilities: the speech box is Llama making a permitted choice and returning a public reason; the function is Python and OpenDSS calculating physical results and enforcing workflow limits; the person is the operator reviewing evidence and retaining operating authority. The Llama wrappers use constrained JSON interpreted by the application, rather than native tool_calls. Language explanations are not proof of physical correctness. In our replay the model may say REVIEW but the human acknowledgment is still PENDING. For each exercise work in pairs: one person runs while the other checks, then swap. Save the input, result, check and next decision. Stanford p.53 separates language understanding from checking a formal decision model in a clinical-trial example. The lab adaptation separates Llama coordination from Python numerical checks and operator review. This lab does not run SMT or MaxSAT, and the analogy supplies no formal guarantee about the grid model.
caption: Our grid teaching adaptation of the language/checking distinction in Stanford Lecture 1, p.53.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.53.

title: Get ready in four small steps
points: Open the notebook, save your copy, connect a CPU and run setup.
Wait for Ready. Then run L0 and L1 before starting the three cases.
note: For a paced workshop, run the setup cell first, then run each named lesson cell when prompted. Runtime > Run all also works, but it reveals later outputs before the prediction questions. The default route needs no GPU, API key or LLM download. If setup stops, reconnect the runtime and rerun setup before starting L0.

title: Run a cell, then read what it returns
points: Find the L heading. Use the play button to run the whole matching code cell.
Wait, then read the table or plot underneath it. Editing an input alone does not update output.
note: Point to the three parts: editable input, run control and returned output. The illustrated input lines are the first two lines of the actual L2 cell, not a complete standalone program. The full cell calls the voltage helper and draws two plots. The runtime remembers variables from earlier cells, which is why we run the lesson in order. If NameError reports a missing variable, return to setup/L0 and rerun the required earlier cells. Do not treat a previously displayed output as the result of a number just edited until you rerun its cell. Use the L labels instead of numerical cell indexes. Later cells need earlier variables.

title: Run L0: choose the classroom route
points: Keep both switches False: new numerical checks, saved controller and archived model replies.
If the data check fails, rerun setup before continuing.

title: Run L1: does the evidence still match?
points: Read binding_pass: does the record match the same inputs and command?
Expect True, False, False. Changing the load or command breaks that match.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L0–L1; cells classroom-002 and classroom-004.
note: Evidence binding means matching a checked record to the exact inputs, proposed command and returned result, using content hashes. Treat L1 as a same-content check, not a test that a physical action passes its limits. The first row keeps the request and command unchanged. The next two rows change a request field or command field, so binding_pass is True, False, False. A failed match calls for new evidence; it does not prove the changed action fails its limits. A matching hash also does not authenticate a sensor.
caption: Reference L1 output: only the unchanged request and command match the evidence.
